finding.claim: Query arguments are never extracted when the request URI has an invalid percent-escape in the path, so ARGS_GET and QUERY_STRING miss the payload.

trace.note: url.ParseRequestURI fails on invalid escape in path
error branch sets urlencodedError, path = uri
ExtractGetArguments only called on success branch, so skipped
queryString set to empty string
repo test marks this as a known bug: /foo%zz?a=b keeps query in REQUEST_FILENAME

finding.guards_checked: urlencodedError is set but nothing in transaction.go denies on it; REQUEST_URI/REQUEST_LINE still contain the raw query so rules targeting those still see the payload. Bypass requires the backend to still serve the request with a malformed path. Not executed; based on code reading and stdlib url semantics.

finding.claim: GET query arguments beyond ArgumentLimit (default 1000) are silently dropped with only a debug log and no inboundDataError flag, so a payload placed after the limit is never inspected.
finding.source: Query-string parameter count and order (e.g. 1000 benign params then &id=<payload>)

trace.note: ExtractGetArguments loops over all parsed values
AddGetRequestArgument entry
checkArgumentLimit returns true when argsGet.Len() >= ArgumentLimit
debug/warn log and early return; value dropped, no flag set
ArgumentLimit default 1000
contrast: body-limit paths set inboundDataError, argument-limit path does not

finding.guards_checked: No inboundDataError or other flag is set on argument-limit overflow; debug logging only. Only the GET path was traced; POST/path variants share the guard but callers were not traced. Not executed.

finding.claim: JSON flattening into a map overwrites earlier values on key collision, so an earlier payload value is never added to ARGS_POST.
finding.source: JSON request body with colliding flattened keys, e.g. {"a.b":"<payload>","a":{"b":"safe"}}
finding.sink: ARGS_POST / json.* collection inspection (col.SetIndex at json.go:35)

trace.note: ProcessRequest iterates flattened map to populate ARGS_POST
res[key]=val overwrites an existing key from a prior path
raw body still stored in json_request_body (not overwritten)

finding.guards_checked: gjson.Valid at json.go:90 does not affect the collision. Raw REQUEST_BODY rules still see the payload, so exploitability requires rules limited to the flattened collection and a backend that reads the literal 'a.b' key or uses first-wins duplicate semantics. Not executed.

finding.claim: @validateSchema ignores its data argument whenever a JSON request body exists, validating the body instead of the targeted value, so a schema-valid body can mask an invalid target value.
finding.source: Valid-schema JSON request body plus a malicious value in a non-body target (e.g. ARGS:foo or a header) to which the rule applies @validateSchema

trace.note: Evaluate(tx, data) entry
reads json_request_body from TX
bodyData non-empty: validates body only
returns !isValidJSON(bodyData); data argument discarded
json_request_body set by JSON body processor

finding.guards_checked: Doc comment at validate_schema.go:26 says body data is retrieved automatically, so precedence may be intentional. Tests at validate_schema_test.go:192 and 202 always pass empty data, so non-body target with JSON body is untested. Requires a rule applying @validateSchema to a non-body target.

finding.claim: @inspectFile treats scanner timeout or execution error as no match, so a deny rule fails open when the external scanner times out or errors.
finding.source: Request value passed as argv to the scanner (controls scan duration); scanner timeout is 10s
finding.sink: Deny decision of a rule using @inspectFile

trace.note: 10s context timeout
value passed as argv element, no shell
timeout or err returns false (no match, allowed)

finding.guards_checked: Fail-open behavior is documented ('false on timeout'), so this is a design weakness. No shell involved; program path comes from rule config. Doc comment at lines 21-23 contradicts code and tests, but that is a doc error, not a security issue. Low severity. Not executed.
